summary: The RADIUS protocol is limited to a total packet size of 4096 bytes. Provisions exist for fragmenting large authentication data using Access-Challenge packets, but not for other kinds of data. This experimental document defines a way to fragment larger amounts of data across multiple packets.

plainLanguage.summary: RADIUS messages cannot be bigger than about four kilobytes, which is too small for some of the authorization information a server now wants to send. RFC 7499 splits such a message into several ordinary RADIUS messages, each carrying a piece. Because every piece is a normal message, the proxies in between do not need to change anything at all.

questions: why is radius packet size limited to 4096 bytes
subtitle: A way to send large amounts of authorization data by splitting RADIUS packets across multiple exchanges.

tldr.problem: RADIUS packets are limited to 4096 bytes, and authentication servers and clients need to exchange large amounts of authorization data that exceed this limit.
tldr.mechanism: RADIUS peers exchange a series of smaller packets called chunks, each containing part of the large data. A new Frag-Status attribute signals when fragmentation is ongoing, and a State attribute ties the chunks together.
tldr.outcome: The only systems that need to change are those that generate or consume the large data; intermediate proxies pass the chunks through unchanged. The document is Experimental.

today: RFC 7499 is an Experimental document that has not been obsoleted or updated. It says the experiment is to check whether the approach is usable at scale by watching how it is taken up in real deployments, and it names the transport of large SAML statements as the main use case so far. It also records two features that still need testing before the document could become a standard: access requests that carry none of the authentication attributes RFC 2865 requires, and the need for proxies to route on the value of the User-Name attribute.

sections.title: The Problem: RADIUS Packets Are Small
sections.content:
RADIUS carries authentication, authorization and accounting information between a client and a server. Each packet is a header plus zero or more attributes, up to a maximum size of 4096 bytes. The limit was there to avoid IP-level fragmentation of the UDP datagram, and 4096 bytes seemed large enough for any purpose at the time.

New scenarios now need to exchange authorization information larger than that. The example the memo gives is the transport of SAML statements from the server to the client, which is likely to exceed 4096 bytes. Peers that want to send large amounts of data have to fragment it across multiple packets. RADIUS-EAP defines how an EAP exchange occurs across multiple request and challenge sequences, but no such exchange is possible for accounting or authorization data.

The three approaches recommended elsewhere in RADIUS do not solve the problem. Using a sequence of packets does not cover data sent from the client to the server, and using names rather than values is hard when the data is highly dynamic, as a SAML statement is. Path MTU discovery does not help either, because it does not allow the sending of data larger than the smaller of the MTU or 4096 bytes. The combination of the size limit and a path MTU that may be far smaller means there is a pressing need for a way to send large amounts of authorization data, and no accompanying solution.
sections.plainLanguage: The four-kilobyte limit was sensible when RADIUS was designed, but modern authorization data does not fit in it. The obvious workarounds each fail for a different reason, so the memo builds the splitting into RADIUS itself.

sections.title: What the Document Covers and What It Does Not
sections.content:
The mechanism should not be used to exchange more than 100 kilobytes of data. Any more than this may turn RADIUS into a generic transport protocol, such as TCP or SCTP, which is undesirable. Experience shows that attempts to transport bulk data across the Internet with UDP will inevitably fail unless they reimplement all the behaviour of TCP, and RADIUS lacks the retransmission policies and congestion control mechanisms that would make it a competitor of TCP.

The scope is limited to authorization data, because the other exchanges do not need it. Authentication exchanges have already been defined to overcome the limit, and since they are the most critical part of a RADIUS conversation it is preferable not to change them. There is no need to fragment accounting packets either, because accounting data is typically composed of many small updates rather than indivisible blocks of more than 4 kilobytes, and the need for large amounts of data per user session is handled by the existing multi-session identifier attribute. Change-of-Authorization packets are not fragmented either; the CoA client sends session identification attributes and a State attribute, and an implementation without fragmentation support responds with a negative acknowledgement and an Unsupported-Service error cause.

The document says the experiment is to verify whether the approach is usable at scale by observing its uptake, usability and operational behaviour in real deployments. It also notes two features that still need testing: the specification may generate access requests with none of the authentication attributes that RFC 2865 requires, and it requires proxies to base their routing decisions on the value of the User-Name attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: This is for authorization data only, and not for bulk transfers: a hundred kilobytes is the recommended ceiling, with the idea that RADIUS should not turn into a file transfer protocol. Authentication and accounting keep the mechanisms they already have.

sections.title: The Chunking Mechanism
sections.content:
Instead of encoding one large RADIUS packet, a series of smaller packets of the same type is encoded, each called a chunk. The encoding is a simple linear walk over the attributes to be encoded, which preserves the order of attributes of the same type as RFC 2865 requires. The number of attributes in a chunk depends on the size limit, the size of each attribute, the number of proxies in the path, and the overhead of the signalling attributes.

The client and the server exchange a series of request and accept packets until all the fragmented data has been transported. Every packet carries a Frag-Status attribute that tells the other party whether fragmentation is desired, ongoing or finished, and each packet may carry the fragmented data or act as an acknowledgement of a chunk from the other side. The chunks are tied together with the State attribute, and each access request carries a User-Name attribute so that the packet can be proxied. The reconstruction is simply appending all the chunks together: unlike IP fragmentation there is no offset field, because the chunks are explicitly ordered and RADIUS is a lock-step protocol, so chunk N+1 cannot be sent until all the chunks up to and including N have been received and acknowledged.

Every packet sent or received as part of the chunking must be a valid packet subject to all format and security requirements. That is what allows a proxy that simply forwards packets to proxy chunks without examining them. The one place where chunking affects the content of an attribute is when a large attribute is split across two chunks, which the Long Extended Type attribute format does not permit; a new T flag in its reserved field marks such a split. The value fields of all attributes remain unchanged, and any per-packet security attributes are calculated for each chunk independently, with no integrity or security checks performed on the reassembled packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The big message is cut into ordinary RADIUS packets, each carrying a marker that says more is coming. The receiver glues them back together in order, one exchange at a time, so nothing has to be reassembled out of sequence.

sections.title: Pre-Authorization and Post-Authorization
sections.content:
An authorization exchange can happen before or after the end user has been authenticated. In the pre-authorization phase, the client may send a large packet of authorization information to the server before authentication starts, and only the client may send authorization data. In the post-authorization phase, the server may send a large packet of authorization data to the client after authentication, and only the server may send it.

In the pre-authorization case the client sends the first chunk as an access request carrying a Frag-Status attribute with the value More-Data-Pending, plus a Service-Type attribute showing that the packet is part of the chunking process. A server that implements fragmentation sees the Frag-Status attribute and postpones all authorization and authentication handling until every chunk has arrived. A server that does not implement it sees a request for an unknown service and returns a rejection, and a client that implements fragmentation must treat such a response as a rejection. A server that wants the rest of the chunks replies with Frag-Status set to More-Data-Request and a State attribute that the client echoes in its next request.

The post-authorization case runs the other way. The server sends chunks as access accepts with Frag-Status set to More-Data-Pending, and the client replies with an access request carrying Frag-Status set to More-Data-Request and the State value from the accept. The last chunk carries no Frag-Status attribute and restores the original Service-Type and State, and the client then processes the attributes as if they had arrived in a single packet. A client that wants to receive fragmented data from the server must say so in its first access request with a Frag-Status attribute set to Fragmentation-Supported, unless the pre-authorization exchange already took place.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two directions. The client can send a big block of information before the user logs in, and the server can send one after. Each side marks its packets as part of a longer exchange and waits for the other to ask for the next piece.

sections.title: The New Attributes
sections.content:
Two new attributes are defined, both taken from the short extended space. Frag-Status has type 241.1 and length 7, and carries a four-byte code whose value says what is happening: 0 is reserved, 1 means Fragmentation-Supported, 2 means More-Data-Pending and 3 means More-Data-Request. It may appear in access requests, challenges and accepts, and must not be included in access rejects.

Proxy-State-Length has type 241.2 and length 7, and carries the total length in bytes of the Proxy-State attributes the server received. This lets the client adjust the size of the chunks it sends. It may appear in access challenges and accepts, and must not be included in access requests or rejects.

A third change is needed elsewhere. A new Service-Type value of 19, Additional-Authorization, marks the packets that belong to a chunked exchange, so that a peer which does not understand the mechanism treats them as a request for an unknown service and rejects them. A new T flag is allocated in the reserved field of the Long Extended Type attribute to mark a large attribute that has been split across chunks. The memo also records that a proxy which cannot add its own Proxy-State attribute to a packet may discard it, which is why the Proxy-State-Length attribute is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Two small attributes carry the signalling: one says how far the exchange has got, and the other tells the client how much the proxies have added. A third marker in the service type tells an old peer that this is not a normal request.

sections.title: Security and Practical Limits
sections.content:
The memo says RADIUS security is already problematic, as earlier specifications have noted, and that this specification changes nothing about it. Every access request associated with fragmentation must be authenticated with the existing Message-Authenticator attribute, which prevents forging and replay to the limits of the existing security.

Sending bulk data does create new considerations. Clients and servers may have to store large amounts of data per session, and that can be significant, so implementations should limit the amount of bulk data stored per session. The method is implementation specific, and section 7 of the document gives some indications of reasonable limits. The bulk data can often be kept outside the memory of the RADIUS implementation, in an external database or in files, which mitigates the resource exhaustion problem, and RADIUS servers already store large amounts of accounting data that way.

Section 7 sets out the practical limits. Implementations must limit the total amount of data sent or received this way, with a default of 100 kilobytes, and must limit the total number of round trips used, with a default of 25. Going beyond either may indicate an implementation error, a misconfiguration or a denial-of-service attack. Both limits should be configurable. The reason for the round trip limit is that an unauthenticated end user can trigger the exchange of large amounts of data, and an attacker could open many connections each asking the server to store a large amount, which could exhaust the server's memory and deny access to real users.
sections.plainLanguage: Each chunk is signed in the usual way, so the existing protection still applies. The new risk is storage, so both the amount of data and the number of round trips are capped, and the caps should be configurable.
